analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA's cross-state smog and soot rule for coal-burning power plants for a decade.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have delayed the EPA's Cross-State Air Pollution Rule until 2022, died in a House subcommittee with no cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred the EPA from putting its Cross-State Air Pollution Rule into effect until the end of 2021. That rule, issued in 2011, cuts fine particle and smog pollution from power plants that blows across state lines into neighboring states. Instead, the bill would have kept the older, weaker Clean Air Interstate Rule in place and barred the EPA from changing it for ten years.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal-burning power plants, which would keep operating under the older, weaker pollution rule and avoid the cost of installing or running scrubbers and other emission controls. Electricity customers in upwind plant states would also avoid some near-term rate pressure, while downwind states kept breathing the pollution.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the EPA from implementing the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule, or any substantially similar rule, before the end of 2021 [S2] [S3].
Keeps the Clean Air Interstate Rule in place through 2021 and prohibits the EPA from modifying it, locking in the older, less stringent controls for a decade [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants, who would continue to breathe fine particle and ozone pollution linked to asthma, heart disease, and premature death. States whose air quality is degraded by other states' emissions would also keep bearing that cost.

drawbacks.text: Delaying the rule for ten years would have left millions of people exposed to higher levels of fine particle and smog pollution from upwind power plants, the exact harm the rule was written to fix [S2] [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection was cost: the compliance deadline would force coal plants to install pollution controls or shut down, and utilities argued the timeline raised electricity prices and threatened reliability. The bill took the opposite extreme, freezing the weaker old rule for a decade rather than adjusting the timeline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls on the health of downwind communities, while the gain goes to plant owners avoiding pollution-control expenses. Even accepting the industry's reliability and price arguments, a ten-year freeze of the weaker old rule, with no EPA authority to revise it, goes far beyond any reasonable phase-in adjustment.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House subcommittee, where it sat until the 112th Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Fincher introduced the bill on September 12, 2011 [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power on September 20, 2011; no further action was taken [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died, the EPA's cross-state air pollution rule was left to proceed, so downwind residents are better off and plant owners avoided no compliance costs. Had it passed, coal plant owners would have been the winners.

for.name: Rep. Stephen Lee Fincher
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to delay the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule and never attracted any cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power and never reported it out; no markup or vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, and it never advanced past a subcommittee referral [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have spared them a decade of costs for cutting fine particle and ozone pollution that drifts downwind. The gain to plant owners comes directly at the expense of air quality for people in neighboring states [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Pollution-control equipment suppliers and scrubber makers
industries.note: A ten-year delay would push off demand for emission-control equipment that the stricter rule would have required. Their interest tracks with cleaner air for the public.
